steps.text: Part 2 of 4: King and rook against king: fence, approach, check on the edge. This part covers Fence and approach. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

steps.caption: Job one: fence. The rook on a4 closes the whole fourth rank, so the black king may only stay above it. Count its squares.

claims.statement: The black king has exactly these five squares.

steps.text: **Fence from far away.** A rook shuts a whole file or rank, and the king may not cross it. Keep the rook where the king cannot reach it, or where your own king guards it. A fence must also move: slide it one line closer to the king and the area he lives in shrinks. That is the whole idea. Watch the fence move in the next three boards.

steps.caption: Fence, part one: the rook slides from file to file, and the black king is driven to the left. White wins by force in at most seven moves.

line.say: The rook closes the e-file from the far end of the board. The black king cannot cross it, and cannot attack the rook.
Black stays on the left of the fence.
The fence moves one file closer. Now the d-file is closed too, and Black has three moves, all to the left.
Black keeps going left, towards the edge.

claims.statement: The whole line is a forced mate in at most seven moves.

steps.caption: Fence, part two: now a check drives the king off the seventh rank and the white king steps up.

line.say: A check along the seventh rank from a square the king cannot reach. Black must leave that rank.
Black steps to the back rank. Ka6 was also legal; this is the engine's line.
The white king steps up. It covers b7 and c7 while the rook holds d7 and d8, so Black has one move.
Forced.

claims.statement: From here White mates in at most six moves.

steps.caption: Fence, part three: the net closes in the corner. One quiet move, then the last check. Mate in at most three moves.

line.say: A check along the back rank. Only a7 is left.
Forced again.
A quiet rook move, not a check. It covers the whole back rank and leaves Black one square, a6.
The only move.
The rook checks along the a-file. The king on c6 covers b5, b6 and b7. Checkmate.

claims.statement: From here White mates in at most three moves.

steps.text: **A rule for the fence [I].** Put the rook on the file next to the black king's file, as far from the king as the board allows. When the king steps away from the fence, bring the fence one file closer. When the king comes next to the rook, move the rook away along its line. A rook left near the king is lost, as the next board shows.

steps.prompt: Before the next card: in the long line you just stepped through, how many of White's eight moves were checks? Write your guess.

steps.caption: The wrong way to fence: the rook stands next to the black king with no guard. It is Black's move.

line.say: The king takes the unguarded rook. Two bare kings are left: a draw.

claims.statement: The rook on e4 is attacked and undefended.
With Black to move, this is only a draw.

steps.text: **Job two: bring your king.** Capablanca's *Chess Fundamentals* (our notes on it) says the rook confines the enemy king to a strip, but only your own king can finish the job. With the enemy king in the centre, he advises walking your king up first, and putting it on the file next to the black king's, towards the centre, not the same file.

steps.caption: If it were Black's move here, the king would have five squares and could walk sideways. Who has the move decides what a check can do.

claims.statement: With Black to move the king has these five squares.

steps.caption: The squeeze, part one. It is White's move and the kings face each other with a gap, so the rook check cannot be answered by stepping forward. Mate in at most nine moves.

line.say: The check comes along the seventh rank from the far side. Black must go back to the last rank.
Black steps back.
The white king walks forward and takes c7, d7 and e7. Black can only slide along the last rank.
Black slides to the other side.

claims.statement: The whole line is a forced mate in at most nine moves.

steps.caption: Part two: the rook waits, the king follows, and the black king is herded toward the corner. Mate in at most seven moves.

line.say: A waiting move [I]: the rook slides along the seventh rank to a square nobody can attack, and Black has to move again.
Black moves toward the corner.
The king follows, covering d7, e7 and f7. Black has two moves, both on the back rank.
Black goes toward the corner.
The rook steps next to the black king, which is safe only because the king on e6 guards f7. Black has one move, h8.
Forced.

claims.statement: From here White mates in at most seven moves.

steps.caption: Part three: the king closes in step by step, and the rook gives the last check.

line.say: The king closes in. Black has one move, g8.
Forced.
The white king takes a position facing the black king, and h8 is the only square left.
Forced.
The rook checks along the back rank. The king on g6 covers g7 and h7. Checkmate.

claims.statement: From here White mates in at most three moves.

steps.text: **Count the checks.** [V] In this line 2 of White's 8 moves are checks; the rest are quiet king steps and rook moves that keep the fence closed. [I] So the king does more of the squeezing, and the rook shuts lines. [H] Beginners overrate checks, because a check feels like progress. A check next to an unguarded rook loses it: see the contrast below.

steps.caption: A quiet rook move can be the strongest move. The white king covers e7, f7 and g7; Black has the d-file left.

line.say: No check. The rook closes the d-file from far away, and Black has exactly one move, f8.
Forced.
The rook checks along the back rank and the king on f6 covers e7, f7 and g7. Checkmate.

claims.statement: Rd1 forces mate on the next move.

steps.caption: Another quiet move: the king on d6 covers c7, d7 and e7, and the rook can wait on the far side.

line.say: No check. The rook closes the b-file from far away, so Black has exactly one move, d8.
Forced.
The rook checks along the back rank, and the king on d6 covers c7, d7 and e7. Checkmate.

claims.statement: Rb4 forces mate on the next move.

steps.text: **Remember.** Fence from far away, and slide the fence one line closer each time the king steps back. Bring your king up beside his. Check only when the kings face each other with one square between and it is your move; otherwise wait with the rook. It fails if the rook stands next to his king with no guard, because he simply takes it.
